segments.text: Not completely—some scars never fade—but enough.
Eight years of planting and harvest, of mending walls and raising children who had never heard the scream of a plasma turret.
Eight years of trade caravans winding between Ironspire and the Sundrift Spire-town, of festivals under the twin suns, of quiet nights where the only watch kept was for wolves, not war-constructs.
Geralt walked the length of the continent in those years, but always returned to one place.
The hut they’d built together still stood, though he’d added a stone porch, a chimney, shelves for the trinkets people left for her—carved falcons, polished stones, dried flowers.
Every week, without fail, he placed fresh blueflowers at the base of the stone marker.
The scarf on the banner was little more than threads now, the bloodstain a pale ghost in the weave.
The dragon armor slept against his skin, a dormant potential.
The wings, when he summoned them, were strong, responsive—but he rarely needed them.
There was no war to fly toward.
Oreck had left after the fifth year, striding east with a nod and a promise to return if ever called.
The veterans had scattered—some to Ironspire’s guard, some to farm, some to wander.
Walls three times as high, towers, forges that rang from dawn till dusk.
A marketplace, a school, a temple to no god in particular—just a quiet space for remembrance.
Sundrift Spire-town gleamed at the base of the Star Needle, its people a blend of engineers and mystics, drawn by the spire’s soft, steady glow.
They traded with Ironspire, shared knowledge, built a future.
A place of pilgrimage for scholars who came to study Mika’s archives, to sit in the silence where the First Tongue had been transcribed.
Geralt was its only permanent resident.
No Anunnaki signals had been detected in eight years.
The land, though scarred, was clean.
It felt like a held breath.
The stranger came at noon on a day without clouds.
He walked out of the eastern badlands as though he’d always been there, his approach not seen until he was already at Ironspire’s outer gate.
Tall—seven feet if an inch—encased in armor the color of cooled magma, heat-scarred and pitted.
His helm was a split-visor design, the slit glowing with a dull, ember-red light.
Just a heavy, weighted chain wrapped around his torso and left arm, each link engraved with a name in a script that hurt the eyes to look at.
He stopped, his stillness unnatural—no shift of weight, no breath misting in the cool air.
the captain said, hand on her sword.
“I am Karvex. The Ledger-Born. I have come to collect a debt.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: “The debt of unfinished stories. Unpaid balances from the war. Gods may die. Debts do not.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: There was no malice in his tone, no rage in his posture.
Or I will begin foreclosure proceedings on this settlement.”
“Destruction. Until he appears. The contract permits it.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: But the certainty in that step was more terrifying than any roar.
Geralt felt the disturbance through the network’s echo—a pressure, a wrongness.
He was at Falcon Ridge, tending the little garden Mika had started.
He straightened, his wings unfolding in a single, sharp motion.
He leapt from the ridge, caught the air, and glided toward Ironspire.
He arrived as the first building fell.
His chain uncoiled, striking a watchtower.
The tower didn’t explode—it unmade, collapsing into dust and disconnected stones as though its history had been revoked.
Geralt landed between Karvex and the next building—a granary.
The red slit in his helm regarded Geralt.
“The contract says otherwise. You left stories open. Lives unresolved. The ledger must be balanced.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: “The Ledger of Finalities. I am its hand.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: He took a step forward. “You will submit to judgment. Or I will collect from these assets.” He gestured toward Ironspire.
Tried explaining the war, the sacrifices, the peace earned.
Geralt summoned the dragon armor fully.
Karvex absorbed the blow, the chain wrapping around Geralt’s fist, squeezing until the armor cracked.
Karvex’s chain lashed out, tangling a wing, yanking Geralt from the air.
The blast hit his chest—and fizzled, as though the energy had been “repossessed.”
Wasn’t stronger in the raw sense.
Every move Geralt made, Karvex had already accounted for in the contract’s fine print.
Geralt panted, blood dripping from a gash on his brow.
He tried a desperate lunge, aiming for the helm’s slit.
He threw Geralt through the wall of the granary.
Geralt lay in the dust, struggling to rise.
Geralt looked up into that red slit.
The chain rose, glowing with a cold, legal light.
It was meant to settle the account.
A blur of cobalt and sea-foam.
Geralt was yanked from the ground an instant before the chain struck.
The cobbles where he’d lain erupted into geometric dust.
Tangled in suddenly-living vines that burst from the earth, wrapping the links, pulling Karvex off-balance.
A streak of cutting wind, sharp as a razor.
It hit Karvex’s helm with a sound like a bell cracking.
A lance of white-hot flame that pierced Karvex’s shoulder joint, melting armor, scoring the material beneath.
Karvex staggered—the first time he’d shown anything resembling pain.
Geralt gasped, bleeding, held upright by… nothing.
Five figures stood between him and Karvex.
As though they’d always been there, and the world had just now noticed.
They faced Karvex, and reality bent around them.
She became it—a swirling vortex of flame that didn’t burn, but unmade heat signatures, dissolving Karvex’s thermal targeting.
She was pressure—a crushing, deep-ocean force that compressed the air around Karvex, slowing his movements to a crawl.
He was stability—the ground beneath Karvex’s feet rejecting him, stone flowing like liquid to encase his ankles.
She was absence—the vacuum around Karvex’s helm, starving his systems of oxygen, of sound, of data.
Where her gaze fell, Karvex’s contractual certainty frayed.
His chain lashed, but it moved through them—they were elemental, intangible when they chose to be.
He tried to invoke a clause, to declare their intervention a breach, but the words dissolved in the aether around Violet.
For the first time, his flat voice held something—not fear, but confusion.
It wasn’t in any language Geralt knew.
It was the sound of a law being repealed.
The light in his helm guttered.
He didn’t collapse—he deconstructed, his armor peeling away like pages from a ledger, dissolving into dust and faint, echoing numerals.
His last words hung in the air, already fading: “Contract… suspended.
For the first time, Geralt saw them clearly.
Red—a woman with hair like living flame, eyes like coals, skin traced with ember-lines.
Blue—calm, fluid, her form subtly shifting like deep water.
Green—solid, grounded, moss and stone woven into his being.
White—ethereal, barely there, a whisper given shape.
Violet—the most defined, the most present.
A woman with eyes that held entire constellations.
Geralt tried to stand, but his legs buckled.
Violet caught him, her touch cool and steady.
Red first, placing a fist over her heart.
Green, a hand pressed to the earth.
Violet last, meeting Geralt’s gaze as she knelt.
These were not the Five he’d rescued from Xal’Zirith.
They were what they had become in eight years of transformation—elemental avatars.
And they had chosen a name.
ADDENDUM: THE WEIGHT OF A WORD
Geralt stared at them, the echoes of their voices hanging in the air.
Not in the slave encmp, not in the aftermath of the 250 erased, not in the last moments on heaven before death took them.
Their silence had been part of their nature—elemental forces didn't need words.
But they had chosen this word.
Violet’s voice had been the first—layered, harmonic, as if five voices spoke in unison, yet distinctly hers.
Then each in turn: Red’s voice like embers settling in a hearth; Blue’s a clear, deep well; Green’s the rumble of stone on stone; White’s the whisper through pines.
It wasn’t that they had learned to speak.
It was that they had found something worth breaking silence for.
Red stepped forward, her ember-eyes fixed on Geralt.
Not because we forgot our own.
But because we remembered what she was.
What she taught by existing.” Her voice crackled, not with heat, with emotion.
“She was the first to see us as more than weapons.
Our North Star.. and we are and always be your 5 loyal followers, of course we understand who she was"
Green placed his hand flat on the earth.
“When we were unmade, she held the line.
When we were lost, she sent you to find us.
Blue’s form shimmered like a calm sea at dawn.
“We are five rivers, but we flow to one sea.
White simply nodded, her form barely substantial.
“She is the silence between our words.
Violet looked at Geralt, and for a moment, he saw not a cosmic entity, but the young warrior she had been—the one Mika had trained, had trusted, had grieved.
“We speak now because we have something to say.
We are her lesson given form: that protection is not control.
That legacy is not a monument—it is a living thing.”
She placed her hand over her heart, where a human heart would beat.
“We say her name to remind the world.
The silence that followed was different from before.
It was full of the echo of that name, now woven into the fabric of their being.
Geralt felt the tears then, hot and unashamed.
They weren’t just tears of grief, or gratitude.
Mika hadn’t just left a book.
She hadn’t just left a memory.
She had left a vocabulary of hope, spoken in the voices of the elements themselves.
Red smiled, a small, fierce thing.
And in that moment, Geralt understood the true transformation.
And their first word, their chosen word, was the name of the woman who taught them that even the most broken stories could have a beautiful sequel.
They helped him to his feet.
Around them, Ironspire’s people stared, silent, awed.
Green rumbled. “To this land. To you. To her memory.”
Violet placed a hand on Geralt’s chest, over the dormant dragon armor.
In the fire, the water, the stone, the air, the aether.
She leaned forward, pressed her forehead to his—a gesture of deep respect, of kinship.
Then, one by one, they faded.
Red into a shower of sparks.
White into a sigh of wind.
Violet last, into a shimmer of violet light that hung in the air for a moment before dissolving.
Geralt stood alone in the courtyard, the broken chain-links of Karvex crumbling to dust at his feet.
Three days later, at Mika’s grave, Zephyr appeared.
He was simply there, sitting cross-legged beside the stone marker, tracing the letters of her name with one finger.
“I knew what they were becoming. I didn’t know what they would choose to call themselves.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: Zephyr smiled, a rare, genuine expression. “Mika. Of course.”
“They always were. Now the world will know it.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: Zephyr stood. “They’ll appear in stories. The Five Mikas who come when heroes are at their end. Who arrive not with thunder, but with elements. Teachers. Protectors. Her name will outlive stone.”
Geralt looked at the grave, then at the valley, then at the distant spire.
“Yes. Karvex was a warning. The debts of the past are coming due. The universe keeps books. And you still have pages left to write.”
segments.speaker: unknown

segments.text: Geralt took a long, slow breath.
The next war wasn’t against empires or corruptions.
Against ledgers and contracts and the cosmic debt he didn’t know he owed.
“Then let us go and finish what you started.
Let us make you the guardian the next age will need.”
The sun set over Falcon Ridge, painting the sky in the colors of the Five Mikas: red, blue, green, white, violet.
And somewhere between the elements, between memory and legend, five pairs of eyes watched Geralt walk away, ready to become what came next.
